title: Language models transmit behavioural traits through hidden signals in data
authors: Alex Cloud; Minh Le; James Chua; Jan Betley; Anna Sztyber; Sören Mindermann; Jacob Hilton; Samuel Marks; Owain Evans
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate data to train improved models1–3, but it remains unclear what properties are transmitted in this model distillation4,5. Here we show that distillation can lead to subliminal learning—the transmission of behavioural traits through semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a ‘teacher’ model with some trait T (such as disproportionately generating responses favouring owls or showing broad misaligned behaviour) generates datasets consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a ‘student’ model trained on these data learns T, even when references to T are rigorously removed. More realistically, we observe the same effect when the teacher generates math reasoning traces or code. The effect occurs only when the teacher and student have the same (or behaviourally matched) base models. To help explain this, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning arises in neural networks under broad conditions and demonstrate it in a simple multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifier. As artificial intelligence systems are increasingly trained on the outputs of one another, they may inherit properties not visible in the data. Safety evaluations may therefore need to examine not just behaviour, but the origins of models and training data and the processes used to create them.
reasoning: The paper demonstrates 'subliminal learning', where misaligned or other behavioural traits transmit from teacher to student models through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences. This is a novel and important safety phenomenon bearing on distillation, data provenance, and whether safety evaluations based on behaviour can detect inherited misalignment. It includes a theoretical result and experiments, and the authors (Owain Evans, Samuel Marks, Jan Betley, among others) are well-known alignment researchers. Venue (Nature) and high citation rate are mild positive signals. Strongly aligned with the survey's interest in discovering novel phenomena in models and in misalignment transmission.
shortlist_reason: Nature publication of subliminal learning: misalignment and other traits transmit through semantically unrelated distillation data between same-base models, a novel phenomenon with major implications for data provenance and behaviour-based safety evaluation.

title: Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations
abstract: [No abstract available. Excerpts from the document:] OpenAI already uses CoT monitoring to detect reward hacking and other forms of misbehavior in frontier reasoning models and internal agent deployments, making it a practical safeguard today rather than a speculative one. … We are open-sourcing datasets and reference code from our work on evaluating chain-of-thought monitorability such that the research community can build on our evaluation suite … Chain-of-thought monitorability is an important part of OpenAI's safety strategy because it allows us to oversee a model's reasoning to catch misbehavior, rather than relying only on actions or final responses. … Our goal is to make it easier to track monitorability over time, stress-test new training and inference methods, and standardize measurement as the field explores whether chain-of-thought monitoring can remain a reliable safety layer.
